meta.description: Not John Adams. Abigail Adams wrote it in a letter to John Thaxter, 29 September 1778, printed in the Adams Papers. Source, context and the mix-up.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If we do not lay out ourselves in the service of mankind whom should we serve?'?
meta.ogDescription: Not John Adams: Abigail Adams wrote it in a 29 September 1778 letter to John Thaxter, signed “Portia” and printed in the Adams Papers.

answer.label: Not John Adams — actually Abigail Adams
answer.authorDates: 1744–1818 · First Lady of the United States, wife of John Adams
answer.sourceLine: Abigail Adams wrote these words, almost word for word, in a letter to her relative John Thaxter. She sent it from Braintree on 29 September 1778 and signed it “Portia.” The letter is printed in the Adams Papers (Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 3, pp. 98–99). No source ties the line to her husband.

source.heading: The 1778 letter

docMeta.dd: Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 3, ed. L. H. Butterfield and Marc Friedlaender (Harvard University Press, 1973), pp. 98–99
Recipient’s copy, addressed “To Mr. John Thaxter Philadelphia”

source.excerpt: It is true says one that Mankind in general are a worthless and ungratefull set of Beings for a Man to wear out himself in serving but if we do not lay out ourselves in the Service of mankind whom should we serve? Our own insignificant selves that would be sordid indeed. Thus I hush all my murmurs by considering we are all embarked upon the same bottom, and if our Country sinks we must sink with it.
trail: The full text of the letter, with its editorial notes, is in the Massachusetts Historical Society’s Adams Papers Digital Edition ↗. It is dated “Braintree Sepbr. 29 1778” and signed “Portia.”
Founders Online (National Archives) gives the printed source as Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 3 (Harvard University Press, 1973), pp. 98–99. See the archived Founders Online page ↗.
Wikiquote’s John Adams page ↗ lists the line under “Misattributed” and credits it to Abigail Adams, letter to John Thaxter (1778-09-29).
Check Your Fact (23 Aug 2019) ↗ checked a Facebook post that credited John Adams. Its verdict was False: the words come from Abigail Adams’s 1778 letter to Thaxter.
source.cutTag: Original spelling, as printed in the Adams Papers
source.excerptNote: The popular version is this sentence from “if” onward. It starts with a capital “If” and puts “Service” in lower case, but the words themselves are Abigail’s. She puts the cynical view in the mouth of an unnamed “one” and offers the question as her answer to it.

author.bio: Abigail Adams (born Abigail Smith) was the wife and closest adviser of John Adams, the second U.S. president, and the mother of John Quincy Adams, the sixth. She wrote a great many letters, often signed with the pen name Portia. They are among the richest records of the Revolutionary era, and the Massachusetts Historical Society publishes them in the Adams Papers.

misattribution.heading: How it became John’s
misattribution.intro: The surnames match and the letter dates from the Revolution, so John Adams gets the credit. In fact the line is Abigail’s, written while her husband was away in public service.

items.why: Check Your Fact ↗ found no similar or matching phrase in John Adams’s writings and traced the words to Abigail’s 1778 letter to Thaxter. Wikiquote’s John Adams page ↗ lists the line as misattributed.

misattribution.truthLine: Abigail Adams wrote it in her letter to John Thaxter from Braintree, 29 September 1778, signed “Portia.” Read the letter in the Adams Papers ↗.

context.heading: A wartime grumble, answered
lead: The letter is less a hymn to service than a complaint she talks herself out of. Abigail tells Thaxter that people at home are “more extravagant, selfish, oppressive than we were last year.” She writes that it “cost me as much to live one month as it used to in a year,” and that she cannot do certain work herself because “they have placed my Husband in a Station that must not be so disgraced.”

She then quotes a cynic, “one” who says mankind is “a worthless and ungratefull set of Beings” to wear oneself out serving, and answers with the famous question. The only other choice, she writes, is “Our own insignificant selves that would be sordid indeed.”
detailsBody: The Adams Papers keep Abigail’s own spelling and capitals (“ungratefull,” “Service of mankind”). The quote as it circulates today is a faithful excerpt. It drops the “but” that opens her answer and modernizes the capitals.
The edition’s notes identify Thaxter’s mother, Anna (Quincy) Thaxter, as Abigail’s aunt. The letter is addressed to him at Philadelphia.
